summary: A 2021 Center for Immigration Studies backgrounder by Steven A. Camarota and Karen Zeigler, using Census Bureau American Community Survey data, finds that immigrants arriving in the U.S. are coming at much older ages than in 2000. The average age of newly arrived immigrants rose from 26 in 2000 to 31 in 2019, though the trend stabilized and 2019 newcomers were slightly younger than in 2017 and 2018. The authors also find the overall immigrant population is aging rapidly, and argue that the trend reduces immigration's modest effect on slowing U.S. population aging and has negative fiscal implications.
one_line: A 2021 Center for Immigration Studies report finds new immigrants arriving in the U.S. are older than in 2000, and the overall immigrant population is aging rapidly.
key_facts: The average age of newly arrived legal and illegal immigrants was 31 years in 2019, compared to 26 years in 2000.
Newly arrived immigrants are defined in the report as those who have lived in the country for 1.5 years or less at the time of the survey.
The share of newly arrived immigrants who were 50 and older was 15 percent in 2019, versus 8 percent in 2000.
The share of newcomers 65 and older was 6 percent in 2019, compared to 2 percent in 2000.
On an annual basis, 224,000 immigrants 50 and older settle in the country, including 172,000 aged 55 and older and 89,000 aged 65 and older.
The average age of all immigrants increased from 39 years in 2000 to 46 years in 2019, more than twice as fast as the average age increase for the nation's overall population.
The number of immigrants 65 and older grew from 3.3 million in 2000 to 7.5 million in 2019, a 126 percent increase.
The number of working-age immigrants aged 18 to 64 grew by 42 percent between 2000 and 2019.
Between 2000 and 2019, the share of new green cards going to parents increased significantly, and the report calls this a likely cause of the rise in arrival age.
The report estimates the annual number of new illegal immigrants in the 2010 to 2018 period at about 600,000, down from roughly 800,000 in the 1990s and 2000 to 2009 period, citing Robert Warren.
The 2017 National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine study found immigrants aged 65 and older were a net fiscal drain in every one of its eight scenarios.
In 2019, 27 percent of immigrants aged 65 and older who arrived in the prior five years were on Medicaid, compared to 13 percent of native-born people in that age group.
In 2019, about 15 percent of immigrants 65 and older who arrived in the prior five years accessed SSI, seven times the 2 percent rate for native-born Americans aged 65 and older.
In 2019 there were 44.9 million immigrants, legal and illegal, in the country.
The immigrant share of the U.S. population aged 65 and older rose from 9.5 percent in 2000 to 13.9 percent in 2019.

entities.name: Center for Immigration Studies
entities.role: publisher of the backgrounder; its research director Steven A. Camarota and demographer Karen Zeigler wrote the report

entities.name: Steven A. Camarota
entities.role: director of research at the Center for Immigration Studies and co-author of the report

entities.name: Karen Zeigler
entities.role: demographer at the Center for Immigration Studies and co-author of the report

entities.name: American Community Survey
entities.role: Census Bureau survey used as the main data source for age at arrival

entities.name: Census Bureau
entities.role: agency that collects the ACS and census data analyzed in the report

entities.name: Robert Warren
entities.role: former INS official, now at the Center for Migration Studies, whose research estimates annual new illegal immigration flows

entities.name: Center for Migration Studies
entities.role: institution where Robert Warren works, per the report

entities.name: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine
entities.role: body whose 1997 and 2017 studies examined the net lifetime fiscal impact of immigrants

entities.name: Medicaid
entities.role: health insurance program for the poor, accessed at high rates by recent older immigrants

entities.name: Medicare
entities.role: insurance program for the elderly, for which recent older immigrants are mostly not yet eligible

entities.name: Supplemental Security Income
entities.role: cash payment program for the disabled and low-income elderly, accessed by recent older immigrants at high rates

entities.name: Great Wave
entities.role: large early-twentieth-century immigration flow whose tail end, ending in the early 1920s, is cited for older immigrants in 1990

entities.name: Great Recession
entities.role: period after which the number of immigrants fell, per the report
